title: AD compromise walkthrough
scenario: Kali to domain controller, one stage at a time
intro: This is a scripted walkthrough of a textbook Active Directory attack inside the homelab, from first scan to lateral movement. It is a scenario, not a live capture: the commands are real but the output is illustrative, and the Security Onion side shows the telemetry each stage SHOULD produce. When I run it for real I'll replace the output with sanitized evidence.

stages.name: Recon
left: 21/tcp open ftp   23/tcp open telnet   3306/tcp open mysql
Nmap done: 254 IP addresses (6 hosts up)
stages.takeaway: A full sweep from one host to a whole subnet is one of the loudest things on a network. Zeek sees the fan-out even without a signature.
stages.fix: Segment so a workstation can't scan servers; alert on connection fan-out; this is why Kali lives on its own leash in the rules.

stages.name: Enumeration
stages.takeaway: RID cycling and null sessions build a user list without a single password. That list is the raw material for everything that follows.
stages.fix: Disable null sessions; restrict anonymous SMB; alert on one source touching many accounts. Account lockout slows password spraying.

stages.name: Credential access
stages.takeaway: Any domain user can ask for a service ticket and crack it offline. The whole attack rides on a weak service-account password.
stages.fix: Long random service-account passwords (or gMSAs); disable RC4; alert on RC4 TGS requests. This is a Security+ favorite for a reason.

stages.name: Exploitation
right: [zeek:smb] write to ADMIN$ then service create
stages.takeaway: A cracked service account with local admin rights turns into SYSTEM on the domain controller through a standard PsExec-style service install.
stages.fix: Least privilege: service accounts should not be local admin on the DC. Alert on 7045 service installs and ADMIN$ writes.

stages.name: Post-exploitation
left: [*] Using the DRSUAPI method to get NTDS.DIT
[*] now I can forge a golden ticket
right: [windows:4662] replication rights used by a non-DC account
a workstation IP speaking a DC-to-DC protocol
= the single highest-signal alert in the chain
stages.takeaway: With directory-replication rights the attacker pulls the krbtgt hash and can mint golden tickets: persistence that survives password resets.
stages.fix: Guard replication rights; alert on 4662 replication by non-DCs and drsuapi from a non-DC host; rotate krbtgt twice if you suspect compromise.

stages.name: Detection and response
stages.attack: Blue team: the whole chain in one view
left: # Pivot the stages into one incident timeline:
# one host, six alerts, one story
right: identify: correlate the six alerts to one source
eradicate: rotate krbtgt x2, rebuild dc01 if golden ticket
recover: restore service, verify clean telemetry
lessons: least privilege + no RC4 would stop stages 3-5
stages.takeaway: The point of the lab isn't the exploit, it's that every stage left evidence. A defender who correlates them sees the whole kill chain from one workstation.
stages.fix: Detection plus response. The containment and eradication steps are the part a SOC analyst actually gets paid for.
